A public benchmark certified 2,638 AI-generated GPU kernels as correct. I checked them with a stricter test and majority of them are not. Here is how I ended up there, because it started somewhere else entirely. I wrote the first native Blackwell tcgen05 training backward for the gated-linear-recurrence family, including the reverse-state stage that is usually run in Triton. One recurrence, five models: fix the gates and you get linear attention, GLA, Mamba-2/SSD, Kimi Delta Attention, and full gated DeltaNet. A single backward trains all of them. The standard check is an approximate-equality test on a few random inputs at one fixed shape. It is cheap and reproducible, which is why everyone uses it. But a kernel can pass that and still quietly return an ordinary number where the real answer is a NaN, or give a different result on every run, or break the moment the input shape changes. So I wrote twelve adversarial gates instead: NaN and infinity handling, determinism across repeats, behavior at shapes I had not tested, whether the accumulator really stays in fp32. Several of them need no tolerance at all, so there is no threshold to argue about. Then I got curious what would happen if I pointed the same battery at other people's kernels. 62.1% carry a contract violation. 39.5% fail a tolerance-free gate, meaning no choice of threshold can excuse them. Head to head, 1,487 pass KernelBench and fail mine, against 14 going the other way. The disagreement is almost entirely one-directional, which suggests a blind spot in what the standard check probes rather than two checks tuned to different strictness. The obvious objection is that I just built a harsher referee, so I tried to make that falsifiable four ways: a 7/7 positive control on kernels I can independently vouch for, a threshold calibration sweep with clean separation on every gate, 98.5% agreement with KernelBench's own correctness code, and a stratified hand-audit. On the kernel itself, the goal was never to be fastest. It was to get the reverse-state stage running native on the tensor cores at all, general across the family, and verified end to end. Speed is future work. The preprint is on Zenodo and I want it on arXiv, but as a first-time submitter I need an endorsement from an established arXiv author in computer science. If that is you, or if you know someone it might be, I would be grateful for a message or an introduction. Link to the paper in the comments. #MachineLearning #GPUComputing #Research

It's surreal to write this post. It's been 8 years ago, when my life completely changed. All I knew about NVIDIA at the time was this magical box -- the GPU — that was producing our papers at University of Toronto. I entered the world of NVIDIA on May 6, 2018 by Jensen’s invitation. And behind the magical box, the magical universe unveiled. The universe of some of the smartest and kindest people I've ever met. People that became my dearest collaborators, colleagues, and friends. A place where a mission unites people and clears all artificial boundaries between teams. A place nurtured by a leader so unique in so many ways that it's almost hard to believe he exists. A place that became more than work, it became my home. We grew the team grounds up, with gravity in Toronto and expanding globally over the years. The mission of the team was to develop new technologies for simulation to power the creation and modeling of virtual worlds. And I couldn't be prouder of what we have achieved. Together, we've learned how to become a research lab in industry. Transitioning from conceptual work we discussed in papers, several of which won best paper awards, to technology that shipped in production and made a real world difference. NuRec, Cosmos, Alpamayo, and OmniDreams are some of the efforts I'm most proud the team has led or contributed to, and so many research works we developed through the years that have empowered them. I'd like to thank everyone for this wonderful journey, especially Jensen Huang , Rev Lebaredian , Bill Dally and Xinzhou Wu who mentored and supported me and the team through the years. But most of all I'd like to thank my team. They’ve made the NVIDIA Spatial Intelligence Lab ( https://lnkd.in/g5DamEbk ) a magical place, a frontier lab in the 3D AI domain, and a kind and collaborative environment where people care about each other and support themselves to drive impact. I couldn't be prouder of what we accomplished and the leaders they have all become. I’ve made the difficult decision to leave NVIDIA. I'm leaving with more love for NVIDIA, so much more than what I came in with. I'll miss you all dearly, and can't wait to see how you continue to change the world 💚 World models is where the next breakthrough lies, and it is around the corner. Our vision started with GameGAN in 2020, where AI reproduced a PacMan game. It was immediately clear this will be the technology to change the game for robotics. DriveGAN (2021) was our first driving simulator fully trained from data. Then came videoLDM (2023) that changed the game for video generation efficiency, Cosmos (2025) as an open world simulation platform for Physical AI, and finally OmniDreams (2026) where for the first time we demonstrated real time interactive driving in a fully AI generated world. I’m super excited for what’s to come.

This is insane...OpenAI open-sourced a Codex plugin for Claude Code 🤯 You can now run Codex inside Claude Code. Code reviews, task delegation, full session handoffs. Two rival agents in one terminal. 100% Open Source. 25,000+ GitHub stars already. Until now the two tools lived in isolation. Claude Code writes the patch, and if you want Codex's opinion, you open another terminal, paste the diff, and explain the whole context again. The plugin adds /codex slash commands directly into your Claude Code session: • codex:review runs a full Codex code review on your current work, same quality as running it in Codex directly • codex:adversarial-review makes Codex actively challenge your implementation, tradeoffs, and hidden assumptions before you open a PR • codex:rescue hands a stuck task to Codex when Claude hits a wall • codex:transfer moves your entire Claude Code session into Codex mid-conversation, context intact Claude can invoke Codex on its own. If it gets stuck during a hard debugging session, it spins up a Codex subagent without you asking. There's also a review gate. Turn it on and Claude cannot finish a task until Codex reviews the change and clears it. A built-in second pair of eyes on every patch. It runs through your local Codex CLI, so your existing ChatGPT subscription covers it. OpenAI shipping an official plugin for a competitor's product tells you where this is heading.
